extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental scientists, and Royal Society readers (17th-century experimentalists and observers)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reporting experimental and observational natural-philosophy work (astronomical observations, mineral/optical experiments, physiological/surgical trials, and practical techniques like desalination) as in Philosophical Transactions (17th century).

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical eclipse observation reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Record precise timings and measures of lunar eclipses (beginning, greatest obscuration, end, whole duration, quantity in 'digits'), and note observational limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: “the beginning of the moon's eclipse was about 2 hours 11 minutes... The greatest obscuration was about 3h. 50m. the end of the eclipse was at 5h. 21 m. the whole duration therefore was 2h. 59m. and the quantity of it was scarce more than 9 digits.” Also note that accurate observation may be prevented by faint earth shadow; report which lunar spots were visible through the shadow and any instrument used (e.g. 20-foot telescope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare observations to predictive astronomical tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Use existing ephemerides/tables (Riccioli's, the Rudolphine tables, etc.) to predict occultations/conjunctions and compare predictions with observed events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: listing times “According to Riccioli's tables... According to the Rudolphin tables...” and noting discrepancies (e.g. a predicted occultation that did not occur). Report predicted separations/occultation magnitudes (seconds/minutes) and whether observation conformed to tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record instrument and observing conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Always report what instrument was used and the atmospheric conditions affecting observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example phrasing: “I had furnished myself with a 20-foot telescope, and though the air was not entirely clear, there being here and there a few clouds, yet Venus and the moon were clearly observed.” Include telescope length, clarity of air, presence of clouds, time of day (daytime sighting noted), and any difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document transient/variable star magnitude over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Report dates and measured magnitudes for new or variable stars and note temporal changes and visibility limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: “The new star... at first appeared of the third magnitude, was in a surprising manner diminished... so that on the 14th of October it could be no longer observed.” Compare to previous years and other nearby stars when assessing magnitude changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental replication and hypothesis testing (viper venom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use repeated experiments, controls, and cross-observer replication to test hypotheses about the seat/nature of venom (yellow liquor vs spirit/‘enraged’ state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes contesting Charas' conclusions and urging new observations: authors “by experiments to confute the opinion... proposes that the authors of the French experiments should make new observations.” Guidance implies: perform numerous, repeatable experiments; compare across species/populations (Italian vs French vipers); record evidence supporting/refuting hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and bioassay of venom samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for collecting, storing, aging, and testing venom, including assessing persistence of toxicity after drying/pulverization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “put up in a glass vessel the poisonous liquor taken out of two hundred and fifty vipers... after the lapse of thirty days, it became dry and friable... pulverized... put into wounds... pullets and pigeons... died.” Guidance: document sample provenance and quantity, storage conditions, transformations over time, and bioassay outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineral/crystal characterization checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize crystals by shape, cleavage, hardness, reactions to heat and acids, electrical properties, optical behavior (refraction, double images), color, surface texture, and behavior when broken or polished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the Iceland crystal account: describe macroscopic habit (rhomboid prism, triangular pyramidal forms), electrical attraction when heated, not easily polished, resists consumption except by strong fire (yields calx like unslacked lime), corroded by aqua fortis, powder color reactions, surface smoothness vs scabrous after hammering, color changes on wetting/drying, occasional rainbow reflections, and optical phenomena (double, sixfold images). Record which tests were applied and results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical experimental controls to distinguish reflection from refraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Design controls that can eliminate reflection as the cause of observed optical phenomena and test whether refraction (including double refraction) explains observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied steps in text: dull the plain sides (to suppress reflection) and observe whether double image persists; break the prism into smaller pieces and test whether the effect scales; consider and rule out internal reflections. If reflection controls fail, investigate refraction patterns and ray behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose and quantify double refraction (disdiaclastic behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate 'usual' and 'unusual' refracted images by their motion/fixity, trace ray paths with varying eye positions, and measure refractive relationships (angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text guidance: observe one image fixed and one movable; test eye at multiple positions to see which image is congruent with reference lines on a table; determine that unusual refraction follows parallels of crystal sides while usual refraction follows surface perpendiculars; measure angle relationships (example found: angle of inclination to angle of refraction as 5:3). Use diagrams and repeated trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for producing fresh water from sea water (desalination principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal methods: freezing (congelation) and distillation; distillation is preferred for general use and should be conducted with particular apparatus and process controls to yield potable water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance in text: freezing yields nearly fresh meltwater but is latitude/season-limited; distillation requires a still or still-head covers, a condenser (worm-tub/cooler), and, when properly conducted, yields water as pure as by congelation. Do not distill to dryness — stop when two-thirds or three-fourths has been distilled because later fractions are less pure and the brine may corrode boilers. Avoid excessive fire which may disengage muriatic acid. Exposure to air often removes empyreumatic tastes; filtration with a particular earth may be used to correct taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipboard distillation apparatus design and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design compact, fuel-efficient distillation setups suitable for shipboard use, using sea-water cooling and space-saving condenser arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: Dr. Irving's improvement replaces small condenser worm-in-tub with a large open pipe kept wet with mops; make the worm pass through a hole in the ship so sea water cools it (saving room and labor of changing cooling water); a properly designed furnace can distil many pots per day with little fuel. Include filtration step to remove tastes, and be attentive to practicalities (savings of room, fuel, and labor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational cautions for seawater distillation
rubrics_metrics.description: Process-control cautions to avoid corrosion, off-flavors, and lower purity in later fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice in text: stop distillation before final fraction (after 2/3 or 3/4); too strong fire or prolonged distillation can produce an unpleasant taste and possibly disengage muriatic acid that corrodes metal; adding potash before distillation might prevent corrosion; often exposure to air ameliorates bad flavor. Bishop of Llandaff's experiments suggest trace saline particles may remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical/physiological experimental method for tracing urine passage
rubrics_metrics.description: Design anatomical experiments using ligatures, careful incisions to avoid cooling internal parts, controlled re-closure, and repeated trials to infer physiological pathways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text method: tie ureters and empty bladder, note bladder after time; avoid crosswise incisions that expose internal parts to cooling — instead use small side openings sufficient to tie ureters and squeeze urine out; resew openings and rehydrate/observe after the animal drinks; press bladder to check for residual urine; repeat experiments for confirmation and note any swelling above ligatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-review criterion: clarity of demonstration and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate mathematical and theoretical works for clarity and preference for direct, intrinsic demonstrations over indirect or reductio ad absurdum arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the review of Elementa Geometriae: value is placed on rendering geometry 'clearer and easier' and giving demonstrations that 'prove the thing in hand by direct and intrinsic principles, not such as are indirect, and leading ad absurdum... whereby it is only concluded that the thing cannot be false, but not shown why it is and must be true.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-review criterion: invitation to observation and quantitative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess experimental tracts by their encouragement of observation and by the provision of quantitative experimental results and estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Boyle's tracts: the purpose is 'to invite the curious to observe the stupendous mutability of the air' and the author provides numerical estimates (e.g. extension ratios like 'as 1 to 2744' and 'about 13000 to 1' for expansion), which are presented to motivate further observation and calculation.
